instruction: Procedural city USD export. `init_file/scene.blend` contains an empty 20 x 20 BU ground plane at Z=0 (with a grey Principled BSDF material `Mat_Ground`), a camera at (15, -15, 20) aimed at the origin, and a sun light. No buildings yet. Units: METRIC / METERS. Your job: open `init_file/scene.blend`, procedurally add 10 buildings, then export the whole scene to an ASCII USD file at `output/city.usda` (relative to the current working directory) with each building's "material ID" encoded as a `custom string material:purpose = "<value>"` attribute on its USD Material prim. ## City layout - 5 x 2 grid: X in {-8, -4, 0, 4, 8} and Y in {-4, +4} -> 10 plots. - Name the buildings `Building_00`... `Building_09`. Column = i%5, row = i//5 (so Building_00 is at (-8, -4), Building_05 is at (-8, +4), etc.). - Each building is a scaled cube: - width = depth = 2.0 BU; - height from this list, indexed by building number: (3, 6, 9, 12, 4, 7, 10, 5, 8, 11) meters; - base sits on the ground (Z=0); center therefore at Z = height/2; top at Z = height. - Apply scale so the mesh carries real dimensions (not a unit cube with a scale modifier). ## Materials - Each `Building_XX` gets its own Principled BSDF material `Mat_Building_XX`. - Base colors are 10 distinct hues. A simple recipe: `HSV((i/10), 0.7, 0.9)` for i in 0..9 (Object Info -> Random -> ColorRamp is also fine if you want a procedural scheme; the evaluator only checks that each material has a UsdPreviewSurface shader emitted). - Tag each material with a custom property `material_purpose`: - even i (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) -> `"residential"` - odd i (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) -> `"commercial"` ## Vertex colors - Each `Building_XX` mesh has a POINT-domain FLOAT_COLOR attribute named `Col`, with every vertex painted a discrete material-ID color: - residential -> (0.2, 0.6, 0.3, 1) greenish - commercial -> (0.6, 0.3, 0.2, 1) brownish ## USD export - File path: `output/city.usda`. The `.usda` suffix forces Blender to write ASCII USD. - Use `bpy.ops.wm.usd_export(filepath='output/city.usda', export_materials=True, export_mesh_colors=True, generate_preview_surface=True, selected_objects_only=False)`. ## Post-process: inject material:purpose into the USDA Blender's USD exporter doesn't automatically map custom properties on `bpy.types.Material` to USDA attributes, so you must post-process the emitted text file to inject the purpose tags. After export, for each `def Material "Mat_Building_XX"` block, insert a line `custom string material:purpose = "<residential|commercial>"` immediately inside the block's opening brace. A regex pass is sufficient: ```python import re purposes = {i: ('residential' if i % 2 == 0 else 'commercial') for i in range(10)} with open('output/city.usda') as fh: text = fh.read() for i in range(10): mat = f'Mat_Building_{i:02d}' pat = re.compile(rf'(def\s+Material\s+"{mat}"(?:[^{{]*?))(\{{)', re.DOTALL) m = pat.search(text) inject = m.group(1) + m.group(2) + f'\n custom string material:purpose = "{purposes[i]}"' text = text[:m.start()] + inject + text[m.end():] with open('output/city.usda', 'w') as fh: fh.write(text) ``` 1. `output/city.usda` exists. 2. First line starts with `#usda` (ASCII USD, not binary `.usdc`). 3. The file contains 10 `def Xform "Building_XX"` prims, with indices 00-09. 4. The file contains 10 `def Material "Mat_Building_XX"` prims, with indices 00-09. 5. `info:id = "UsdPreviewSurface"` appears at least 10 times (one per material). 6. `material:purpose` appears at least 10 times. 7. Parsing all `material:purpose` string values yields at least 2 distinct entries (e.g. `{residential, commercial}`). 8. `primvars:displayColor` is present (Blender emits this when `export_mesh_colors=True`). 9. Building height variation: parsing the `extent = [...]` blocks gives a set of Z-extents whose standard deviation is at least 2.0 -- or, as a fallback, the file carries at least 10 distinct `xformOp:scale` triplets.
source: Parish, Müller 2001 — "Procedural Modeling of Cities", SIGGRAPH; Pixar USD Specification
